title: Block: Iterative DFS With a Stack
oneLiner: Return the order a depth-first search visits nodes from a start, using an explicit stack instead of recursion.
keyTakeaway: With an explicit stack, check visited when you pop and push neighbours in reverse. That reproduces the recursive order exactly, and it never overflows the call stack.
explanation:
adj[i] lists node i's neighbours in the order to explore them. Return the nodes in the order a recursive DFS from start would first visit them: visit a node, then fully explore its first unvisited neighbour, then the next.

Keep a stack that starts with start. Pop a node; if it was already visited, skip it. Otherwise mark it, record it, and push its unvisited neighbours in reverse order, so the first-listed neighbour is on top and popped next.

Why check on pop here, when BFS marks on push? A node can be pushed by an early neighbour and reached sooner through a deeper path; marking at push time would lock in the early position and give a different order from recursion. Checking on pop costs a few duplicate stack entries and gets the depth-first order right. Grids, flood fills and anything deep enough to overflow recursion use this block.

starterCode.python:
def dfs_order(adj, start):
    # 1. Make an empty visited set, an empty order list, and a stack holding the start.
    # 2. While the stack is not empty, pop a node; skip it if it was already visited.
    # 3. Mark it visited and append it to the order.
    # 4. Push its unvisited neighbours in reverse, so the first-listed neighbour is popped next.
    # 5. Return the order.
    return []

gotchas: Pushing neighbours in listed order, which explores the last neighbour first.
Marking visited on push, which gives a different order from recursive DFS on graphs with cycles.

complexity.note: Every node is visited once and every edge pushes at most one stack entry, so the stack can briefly hold O(E) entries; the visited set is O(V).
